newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa mutiny worsens, curfew in capital.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa mutiny worsens, curfew in capital.

text.p: Army mutineers in Central African Republic clashed with loyalist soldiers in the capital Bangui as the country's president ordered a night curfew and warned he would use force if the rebellion did not end.
Hospital sources on Sunday said three civilians were killed and 22 wounded during fighting between troops loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse and those who demand Patasse's resignation.
Rebel sources said the dead were presidential guards and claimed they were holding 15 loyalist troops ambushed as they readied to attack a rebel stronghold in southern Bangui.

In a radio and television address on Saturday night, Patasse announced the night curfew in the capital Bangui and hinted he would use force to put down the third army mutiny this year. French troops based in Bangui under bilateral accords helped quell a more serious uprising in May.
Church-mediated talks between the government and soldiers have been blocked by rebel demands for Patasse's resignation, something the president has rejected.
Patasse repeated his call on mutineers to lay down their weapons unconditionally.

"In my position as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, I could indeed have ordered military operations to bring this rebellion to an end, but it would have brought harm to the civilian population," Patasse said. "Thus I was patient. I issue two demands: lay down your arms - immediately and unconditionally," he told mutineers.
Mutineers hold the main Kassai military barracks outside Bangui and the armoury there. Loyalists in Kassai have joined pro-Patasse forces in the Camp de Roux near the city centre.

Rebels have complete control of southern and western Bangui. Outside the capital they hold sway in Lobaye barracks in the south and Boumbari and Bangassou near the eastern border with Zaire, home of Yakoma elements loyal to former president Andre Kolingba.
Meanwhile, terrified residents have been fleeing out of the capital to avoid clashes.
"The rebels are well armed and the mutiny appears to have taken root," a military source said of sporadic gunfire heard in the capital after Patasse's address.
Soldiers have hardened long-running grievances over pay and status into political demands, which have split the army between troops from Patsse's northern region and those from the south.
Southerners are suspected of allegiance to Kolingba, one of candidates defeated by Patasse in multiparty elections in 1993.

The tribal dimension has stoked fear of civil war in the impoverished country better known for the excesses of its former self-styled emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who died in October. A state funeral for Bokassa has been held up by the mutiny.

France reinforced its garrison in Bangui after the uprising started on November 16. But unlike their robust intervention in May with helicopter gunships and armoured vehicles, the French appear to be avoiding clashes with rebels this time.
